title: "Workspace, Attempts, Receipts, and Artifacts"
subtitle: "How is durable evidence appended and resolved safely?"
toc-depth: 2

**Status:** `CONVERGING` implementation design.

## Bind one leaf workspace to one Plan

A V1 replaceable workspace is a relocatable stable root pointing to one leaf
with one sealed Plan plus append-only request attempts. Each request carries
its own semantic runtime:

```text
.scnsim.lock                    # persistent advisory-lock inode
workspace.json                 # replaceable root and active-leaf pointer
leaves/<leaf-instance-id>/
  workspace.json               # immutable Plan binding
  plan.json
  requests/<request-sha256>/
    request.json
    attempts/.staging-000001-<lowercase-canonical-uuidv4>/
    attempts/000001/
      attempt.json
      logs/
      artifacts/
      outcome.json
      result.json
      receipt.json
```

The workspace location is not part of computational request identity. It
selects the evidence store in which that request must be found; relocating the
whole verified workspace does not rename the request. All stored paths are
relative to the workspace. `receipt.json` is written last and only after Python
verifies the attempt outcome. It seals success, typed failure, or interruption;
only a verified success receipt can materialize an `AnalysisResult`. A
temporary staging directory is never a successful analysis Result.

V1 uses one writer lock per workspace; different workspaces may run in
parallel. This deliberately simple ceiling avoids two processes selecting the
same next attempt number or sealing competing successes. Per-request locking
is considered only if measured same-workspace throughput requires it.

On Linux and macOS the stable root permanently retains `.scnsim.lock` and uses
stdlib `fcntl.flock`: writers take an exclusive lock and `resolve()` takes a
shared lock. The file is never deleted or replaced; normal exit, crash, or
process termination releases the kernel-held lock. Windows fails before any
workspace mutation.

The writer lock spans Plan binding or replacement, attempt-ordinal allocation,
child execution, staged-artifact promotion, outcome verification, and receipt
sealing. `resolve()` takes the same lock only long enough to read one stable
hash chain; it never holds an execution slot.

## Iterate topology in one workspace {#iterate-topology-in-one-workspace}

`CircuitRun(..., versioned=False)` is the default Notebook behavior. The root
contains an atomically replaced JSON active-leaf pointer. Its canonical target
is `leaves/<leaf-instance-id>`; no filesystem symlink is used. Reopening
the same path with the same Plan identity reuses its evidence. A different Plan
is validated and sealed first. Under the exclusive lock, Python completes a
sibling staged leaf, atomically renames it to `leaves/<new-leaf-instance-id>`,
atomically replaces the root pointer, and only then removes the prior leaf. No
prompt, recycle area, or implicit topology history is added. A prior Run or lazy Result
whose bound leaf `workspace_instance_id` or Plan no longer matches that path
raises
`WorkspacePlanReplacedError` instead of reading unrelated evidence.

Every replacement creates a new evidence-only leaf instance ID. This keeps an
old Run stale through an `A → B → A` topology sequence instead of accepting the
later A workspace merely because its Plan hash matches again.

With `versioned=True`, the selected path is a parent index:

```text
workspace.json
iteration01/
  workspace.json
  plan.json
  requests/...
iteration02/
  workspace.json
  plan.json
  requests/...
```

Each `iterationNN` is an ordinary leaf workspace. The parent maps exact Plan
hashes and leaf instance IDs to monotonically assigned directories, using at least two decimal
digits. Reopening the same Plan reuses its existing iteration; only a new Plan
identity allocates the next ordinal. Specs and ParameterSets remain requests
inside that iteration.

Index entries are stored in ascending ordinal order. Ordinals and directories
are unique, every Plan hash appears once, and `next_iteration` is one greater
than the greatest existing ordinal (or `1` when empty). These cross-entry
invariants are semantic validation in addition to the JSON Schema shape. A
replaceable root, a versioned parent, and all leaf workspace-instance IDs under
that root are mutually distinct; every pointer/index entry repeats the exact
child leaf ID it names.

Opening an existing replaceable root with `versioned=True` is a supported,
atomic one-way conversion: its active leaf becomes `iteration01` and the
versioned parent index replaces the root pointer without changing that leaf's
instance or request identities; the new parent receives its own instance ID. Opening a
versioned parent with `versioned=False` raises
`WorkspaceVersioningDowngradeForbidden` before mutation. The message explains
that versioning was an explicit preservation choice and directs the user to a
different workspace path for replacement mode.

A pre-upgrade Run follows its preserved leaf instance into `iteration01` after
the conversion. It does not become stale merely because the user enabled
preservation; subsequent replacements of that leaf remain detectable by its
instance ID.

## Reuse success and append failure history

The request directory is derived from canonical request identity. If one
attempt contains a complete verified success, the terminal operation returns
it. Otherwise a new call appends the next immutable attempt. Failed and
interrupted attempts remain visible to `inventory()` and cannot be overwritten.

A verified `HBBatchResult` is successful request evidence even when every case
contains a numerical `HBCaseFailure`; repeating it reuses the batch. Only a
request-level failure or interruption is retryable.

`resolve()` acquires no execution slot. It recomputes the request identity,
finds the verified success, and validates Plan, semantic runtime, receipt, manifest, and
artifact hashes. Missing or corrupt evidence is an error; it never falls back
to another attempt or request.

## Inspect one bound leaf without selecting it {#inventory-one-bound-leaf}

`run.inventory()` is pure workspace inspection. It takes the persistent
workspace lock in shared mode while it resolves the Run's leaf and verifies the
request/attempt chains, then releases the lock before returning. It takes no
execution slot, launches no child process, creates no request or attempt,
cleans no staging directory, changes no root pointer or index, and writes
nothing.

Inventory operates on exactly the leaf bound to the invoking Run. At a
replaceable root it inspects only the current active leaf and verifies that the
leaf instance ID and Plan still match the Run; a stale Run raises
`WorkspacePlanReplacedError`. A versioned Run inspects only its own retained
iteration, including `iteration01` for a Run preserved by the supported
one-way upgrade, and never scans sibling iterations.

Within that leaf, inventory verifies every request directory against its exact
`request.json` hash and Plan binding. Request rows are ordered
lexicographically by `request_sha256`. Canonical hidden staging directories are
ignored for listing and status and are left untouched; malformed staging names
retain the existing integrity failure behavior. Every visible final attempt is
validated against the existing attempt, outcome, Result, and receipt contracts,
and its ordinal text is listed in numeric ascending ordinal order.

A request is `succeeded` when any attempt contains a complete verified success.
This includes a verified HB batch whose every case is a numerical
`HBCaseFailure`. Without a verified success, the request status is `failed` or
`interrupted` according to the sealed outcome of the greatest finalized
ordinal. A request directory with no final attempt after hidden staging entries
are ignored, any broken request/attempt/receipt hash chain, or any invalid
final attempt raises `EvidenceIntegrityError` for the whole inspection;
inventory never skips the bad request or returns a partial listing.

The returned `InventoryResult` remains inspection output, not a request
selector. `resolve()`, `build_report()`, and every other public API refuse to
consume it as a latest or current request; resolution still requires the exact
Ref, Spec, and ParameterSet contract, and reports still require explicit
receipt-backed analysis Results.

Optimization adds one immutable, hash-linked ledger per completed generation.
The ledger records package-visible optimizer coordinates, population ordinals,
physical bindings, objective components, cache/failure state, and the prior
ledger hash. It separately binds the canonical raw and transformed population
hashes. It does not serialize package-private optimizer state. Retry
selects the greatest verified compatible generation, restarts the pinned
optimizer from the same seed, and replays ledger costs only when coordinates,
generation, and population column match bitwise. Equal ordinals with different
hashes or any replay mismatch are `EvidenceIntegrityError`; an interrupted
generation is discarded and deterministically replayed.

## Promote one attempt atomically

Attempt staging is always a sibling of the final ordinal directory. For
positive numeric ordinal `k`, its path text is `str(k).zfill(6)`: `1` becomes
`000001`, while `1000000` remains `1000000`. The two names are therefore
`requests/<request-sha256>/attempts/.staging-<ordinal-text>-<uuidv4>/` and
`requests/<request-sha256>/attempts/<ordinal-text>/`. The staging suffix must
match lowercase canonical UUIDv4 form; a short ordinal, uppercase UUID, wrong
version/variant nibble, or mismatch with `attempt.json.ordinal` is invalid
evidence rather than an alternate spelling.

Julia writes only inside that staging directory. Python validates the outcome
and allowed artifacts, writes
`receipt.json` last, fsyncs the written files and directories, then atomically
renames the staging directory to the final ordinal name on the same filesystem.

A valid `outcome.json`, logs, and referenced artifacts move with that rename;
the receipt records the outcome SHA-256. Invalid raw outcome bytes may be moved
under `logs/`, but the final attempt cannot retain them under the authoritative
`outcome.json` name. Interruption never promotes an unverified Result. Hidden
staging left by a crash is neither an attempt nor a Result and is removed by
the next exclusive writer before allocating a new ordinal.

## Store arrays without pickling

Scalar metadata, schemas, failures, and receipts use canonical JSON. Large real
arrays use Zarr V2 chunks; complex arrays use paired Float64 real/imag arrays
with one typed manifest. V1 starts with uncompressed chunks so another language
can implement the format without a codec dependency. The OGC-endorsed
[Zarr V2 standard](https://www.ogc.org/standards/zarr-storage-specification/)
defines JSON metadata and optionally compressed binary chunks for
multidimensional arrays.

Chunk shape, array order, dtype, axes, units, coordinate IDs, and real/imag
pairing are manifest authority. A Python Result may load chunks lazily, but
must reconstruct the declared NumPy/Pint surface before returning it.

Julia alone creates `.zgroup`, dataset `.zarray`, and chunk files. Python is an
exact validator and reader: it rejects any metadata byte difference, missing or
extra path, invalid chunk name/length, or manifest/hash mismatch and never
rewrites the tree through a Zarr library. The root-group/dataset layout and
exact compact no-newline metadata bytes are fixed in
[Canonical Identities and Schemas](canonical-identities-and-schemas.qmd); no
`.zattrs`, `.zmetadata`, sidecar, or other extra is permitted.

The exact envelopes and Result/artifact references are defined by the
[machine-readable identity schemas](canonical-identities-and-schemas.qmd).
